A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WSPO research, with matching core equations and experiments. Their text, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison. V1's example-generation appendix is retained as Appendix G in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original Qwen training and evaluation results for summarization, dialogue, instruction following and reasoning, together with sensitivity analyses and generated examples.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds Llama, vision-language, rejected-response, equal-size transfer, SimPO and training-time results.

M1.justification: The weak-model log-probability ratio, WSPO squared loss, regularization parameter and optimization procedure remain unchanged. V2 applies the existing method to additional model configurations and modalities without documenting a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds image-text preference training on RLHF-v and evaluation on MMHal-Bench for informativeness and hallucination. This substantially extends the original text-only coverage to vision-language tasks. Existing training datasets and benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: SimPO becomes an evaluated comparator in Appendix F.1, Tables 12–13; v1 only cited it. Existing SFT, DPO and PPO comparisons remain, and Appendix F.2 adds a PPO–WSPO timing comparison. The main comparator addition is therefore one optimization method.

E3.justification: V2 adds Llama and vision-language model configurations, rejected-response training, equal-size 7B transfer with varying gamma, and SimPO parameter settings. New protocols include MMHal-Bench metrics and timing at batch size 32, sequence length 4K and 5,724 steps. These are additional experimental designs; the original evaluation settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: New Appendices C, D and F investigate dependence on preferred training responses, transfer when teacher and student have equal size, sensitivity to SimPO settings, and computational efficiency. These substantially expand the original weak-model-size, gamma and SFT analyses. Existing case studies are retained in Appendix G.

E5.justification: The summarization results retain averaging over three samplings and error bars, and Table 3 retains identical uncertainty reporting. V2 introduces no new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or defined uncertainty-estimation procedures; the new timing range is not identified as such an estimate.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces all five MMLU scores and corresponding averages: Qwen2-7B-Instruct changes from 45.31 to 69.94, for example. The reason is unexplained despite unchanged stated zero-shot evaluation, so these are revised reports rather than demonstrated model improvements. Tables 7–14 add substantial results, including Llama3.1-8B WSPO's 57.20 Arena-Hard win rate and MMHal-Bench scores of 4.02 informativeness and 0.22 hallucination. Table 1 remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, Proposition 1, the WSPO objective and Appendix A derivations retain their mathematical substance. Proposition 1 and the composite-reward discussion move from Section 3.1 to Appendix A.2. Added notation explanations and equivalent formatting of gamma do not introduce new theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about transferring and amplifying weak-model alignment while preserving strong-model knowledge. The headline Arena-Hard, AlpacaEval 2 and MT-Bench claims are unchanged; the new experiments chiefly provide additional support.

C2.justification: V2 adds a tentative model-capacity explanation for amplification and claims reduced overfitting and reward-hacking risks. Appendices C–F substantially expand interpretations concerning rejected-data suitability, equal-size alignment control, applicability beyond text models, and memory and tuning trade-offs. Appendix F also proposes WSPO before PPO while recognizing PPO's ability to explore beyond the dataset distribution.

D1.justification: Appendix F documents SimPO hyperparameters, reward-model construction, 80GB GPU memory, timing configuration and measured training times. These provide additional reproducibility information for the new comparisons. Existing training descriptions, prompts, software references and code-access link are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds Zhou et al.'s weak-to-strong search to Section 6.2 and references supporting Llama, RLHF-v and MMHal-Bench. Appendix F develops a focused comparison with the already-cited SimPO. The broader related-work structure and research positioning remain intact.

P1.justification: V2 clarifies method notation and reorganizes experimental setup paragraphs under Task, Models and Evaluation labels. It relocates the proposition discussion, inserts new appendix sections and updates affiliations, publication headers and acknowledgments. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 7–14 introduce displays for Llama transfer, rejected data, equal-size transfer, vision-language evaluation, SimPO and training time, substantially expanding the comparative presentation. Figure 1 is reduced and moved onto the first page, and Table 2 is relocated. Existing figure graphics are unchanged; example tables are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support beyond v1's Qwen text-model experiments. Llama and vision-language evaluations test broader applicability, while rejected-response and equal-size transfer studies directly probe what the method requires. These address important gaps in validation. Unexplained MMLU revisions and limited uncertainty and protocol detail for some new comparisons constrain confidence, but do not outweigh the substantial additional evidence.
